k204: Two buyers in the same Durrës building can end up with completely different outcomes because one bought a finished apartment with its paperwork in order and the other bought a floor plan. The zone was identical. The risk was not.
k205: This is our type-by-type assessment for 2026. Confidence is moderate: these are judgements about structure and incentives, informed by market data, not guarantees about individual buildings.
k207: Approach with caution, and only with developers whose completion record you have personally verified.
k208: The structural issue is that Albania has no escrow requirement. In markets with escrow, your money sits with a neutral party and is released against construction milestones. In Albania it goes to the developer, who is also the party whose solvency you are betting on. If the project stalls, you are an unsecured creditor of a construction company.
k209: The 20-30% discount to a completed unit is real, and it is not a gift. It is the market pricing that risk. The question to ask is not whether the discount is attractive but whether this specific developer has delivered comparable projects on time, and what happens to your deposit if they do not.
k210: Buying off-plan in 2026 has one additional consideration: transaction volumes are down about 35% year on year, which is exactly the environment in which pre-sale-funded developers run short of cash.
k211: Completed new build with leje përdorimi
k212: This is the best risk-adjusted purchase in the market, and it is where we would put a first-time buyer without hesitation.
k213: The leje përdorimi — the certificate of use — is the document that confirms the building was completed lawfully and may be occupied. With it, the construction risk is gone, the unit can be rented immediately, and the title path is clean. The premium over off-plan is genuinely earned.
k214: If you take one thing from this article: ask for the leje përdorimi by name, and do not accept "it is coming" as an answer.
k216: Avoid in seismic zones. Treat with care in Tirana.
k217: The 2019 earthquake changed how Albanians price older construction, and it did so permanently. Pre-2000 buildings were largely built under standards and supervision that no longer inspire confidence, and the discount they carry reflects a real difference in structural risk rather than a market inefficiency waiting to be arbitraged.
k218: In central Tirana some older stock is worth owning for location and plot value. On the coast, in the zones that shook, we would not.
k220: Neutral, with a clear warning about the arithmetic.
k221: Penthouses command a 20-40% premium. Rental income does not rise proportionally — tenants pay for bedrooms and location far more than for a top floor and a terrace. That makes the penthouse premium a lifestyle purchase that happens to be in an investment article.
k222: Buy one because you want to live in it. Do not buy one expecting the premium back on exit unless the building is genuinely prime.

k226: The trade-off is liquidity: fewer buyers means a longer sale. This is a hold, not a flip.

k229: There is nothing structurally wrong with the product. There are simply not enough transactions to establish a reliable price or a dependable exit, which makes it hard to know what you are buying at and harder to know what you will sell at.
k231: The highest upside on this list and the only one we would not touch without a lawyer.
k232: The issues are title history, agricultural classification and restitution claims — the last being the legacy of ownership transfers going back decades that remain unresolved in parts of the country. Any of the three can make a plot unbuildable or unsellable, and none of them are visible from a photograph.
k233: Handled properly, with the legal work done before money moves, land offers the largest gains available in this market. Handled casually, it is the fastest way to lose the entire amount.

k256: Durrës Beach or City Centre: Where's Actually Better to Live?
k257: The centre if you are going to live there, the beach if you are buying a season. Currila and Vollga hold the year-round population and the Tirana commuters. Plazh and Golem are built around summer, took the worst of the 2019 earthquake, and Golem's sewage problem is documented and still unresolved.
k259: The city centre — Currila, Vollga, the older core of Durrës — is where local families live and where people who commute to Tirana for work tend to settle. The beach zone, Plazh and Golem, is built around a different population: short-term-rental guests in summer, and a resident base that's thinner and more seasonal. Neither is "better" in the abstract; they're built for different lives, and conflating them is where a lot of buyer disappointment starts.
k260: The numbers back this up. Durrës's population has fallen by roughly 21,000 since the 2011 census — local demand for year-round housing isn't growing the way tourist demand for the beach strip is. And ownership on the beach side skews heavily toward <s1>short-term-rental investors</s1> rather than residents: historically, more than half of the businesses and units along the Golem/Plazh strip trace back to Kosovar buyers and diaspora investors buying specifically for Airbnb income, not to live in themselves. That's not a criticism of the zone — it's a straightforward explanation for why it feels different day to day than the city centre does, even before you account for the seasonal noise.
k261: The earthquake still shapes which zone feels safer
k262: The 26 November 2019 earthquake, magnitude 6.4, was centred near Durrës — 51 deaths nationally, over 14,000 damaged buildings, more than €1 billion in damage. The worst of it landed squarely on the beach-facing zone: buildings collapsed specifically in Plazh and Shkëmbi i Kavajës. Four years on, roughly 2,500 families were still without permanent housing, and the market's own memory of it hasn't faded — post-earthquake new construction carries a real, lasting price premium over older beach-zone stock, and that premium isn't just sentiment. Year of construction and seismic standard are worth asking about on every unit here, not only the ones near the water — a document, not a feeling, is what actually confirms it.
k263: The beach zone's open problem: what's actually in the water
k264: Golem's beach has a documented sewage discharge problem, reported repeatedly and still not fully resolved by an unfinished World Bank-linked remediation project. Durrës and Golem hold no Blue Flag certification — the only Blue Flag beach on this entire stretch of coast is Palasë, well south, near the Riviera. It doesn't rule Golem out, but "beachfront" is doing real unearned work in a lot of the marketing copy for this zone, and it's worth knowing before you commit to a lifestyle built around swimming there daily.
k265: The commute, if the real choice is Durrës versus staying in Tirana
k266: Road access to the capital runs 30 to 60 minutes depending on traffic, with roughly 41 buses a day running the route already — a real commute, not a theoretical one. It's also a cheaper one: Tirana rent runs roughly 57% higher than Durrës's for a comparable flat, which is most of the actual financial case for living in Durrës and commuting rather than living in the capital outright. <s1>The Tirana–Durrës railway, once it's actually running, shortens that same trip to 22 minutes</s1> — a real near-term catalyst for anyone weighing this decision today.
k267: The title risk that's concentrated, not spread evenly
k268: Roughly 25 years of building permits were issued for six-to-eight-plus-storey buildings in Golem and Shkëmbi against a legal limit of three storeys — a specific, documented pattern of illegal extra floors concentrated in the beach zone, serious enough that commune heads have faced arrest over it. This is a title-clarity risk that doesn't apply evenly across Durrës; it's worth a harder look specifically on beach-zone buildings than on a city-centre flat.
k270: If daily life, a real commute option and a stable resident community matter most, the city centre is built for that in a way the beach zone genuinely isn't. If the plan is coastal life with the trade-offs named above — seasonality, the sewage issue, and the illegal-floor pattern to check for specifically — Plazh and Golem are still the more affordable entry point onto this stretch of coast. <s1>The purchase mechanics are identical either way.</s1>
